#10500. Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's new efficient embedding model

Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking new possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

Building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

Afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as big on this task.

EmbeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

Beyond the new Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

The EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

The model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

EmbeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

The results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

EmbeddingGemma is integrated with many popular tools, making it easy to incorporate into your existing workflows and applications. The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

Regardless of your framework choice, you should be mindful of the prompts. For embedding models, prompts are prepended to the input text to allow the model to distinguish between different tasks. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

If you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

You can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below shows usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

As with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

Below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

This code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

This code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

This code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

It's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

Note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

#10499. Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations

Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

The supply of this tiny module (or lack thereof) could derail the hundreds of massive data centers planned in the U.S.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microsoft, the tech giant that is building 35 data centers around the U.S. and has plans for 134 more, has reportedly met with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council as the FCC is considering an import ban on Chinese optical transceivers. According to Reuters, the company, alongside the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), is lobbying against the move.

“It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt,” ITI Executive Vice President of Policy and General Counsel John Miller said. He also added, “Those chips, without optical transceivers, literally could just sit there waiting around unutilized until you actually have the transceivers to essentially connect them together,” referring to the AI chips that data centers use.

Optical transceivers are tiny modules plugged into hardware that convert their electrical signals into light signals, allowing data to be transmitted as light pulses across fiber optics. Data centers increasingly use optical transceivers and fiber optics to transmit data between AI GPUs and server racks, as they’re faster, offer lower latency, require less power, and generate less heat compared to traditional copper connections. However, Chinese companies currently supply 66% of the global market, meaning banning them from supplying data centers in the U.S. would more than halve the available supply, thereby exacerbating the various shortages that have been pummeling the industry.

However, there are concerns that some of these transceivers could be compromised by Beijing and be used to steal data, install malware, or remotely disrupt American data centers, which is why the FCC is considering the restriction, just like how it banned Huawei from the U.S. telecommunications network. But unlike Huawei, which had many established competitors in the telecommunications hardware industry, only two U.S.-based companies produce optical transceivers that data centers need — Coherent and Lumentum. While these firms could produce optical transceivers to compete with Chinese offerings, they simply do not have the scale to make up for the shortfall if the FCC bans Chinese imports today.

One compromise floated by the Trump administration is that it would only ban Chinese optical transceivers capable of hitting 3.2 terabits per second. While this technology already exists, its production isn’t expected to expand until 2028, with installation not beginning until 2029. This should give American producers time to ramp up their own output, although the suggestion is still under consideration.

#10497. AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Submarine AI laser robots have been a surefire success for Norwegian salmon farmers, according to the most recent annual report from the aptly named Stingray Marine Solutions. The Oslo, Norway-based firm now has over 3,500 units deployed around salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish. Stingray deployments are up by about 1,000 over the last year. This operation has grown to become one of the largest commercial AI deployments in Scandinavia.

These high-tech AI-enhanced submarines protect 20-25% of farmed salmon in the country, according to the latest figures. Using this high-tech AI laser solution to ‘optically delouse’ the salmon means fish don’t have to be passed through harsh chemical baths to prevent infestations of these tiny parasitic crustaceans. The result is improved salmon growth and welfare, and consistently cleaner fish exhibit reduced mortality.

The video above shows a behind-the-scenes peek at the 250-employee-strong Stingray operation. There’s some colorful laser action with two Stingrays seen zapping away in a salmon pen included in the clip. They use AI to recognize and target the sea lice.

Sea lice are a big problem for fish farmers, with the control of these parasites being a central challenge for the industry. Traditionally, measures such as chemical treatments were used to help control the buildup of sea lice. However, while chemicals can treat a large number of fish simultaneously, they can be bad for the environment, can stress fish, lice can develop resistance, and the introduction of any kind of poison or toxin into food production isn’t usually good for humans either.

In contrast, the Stingray AI laser system identifies and targets only sea lice, works continuously 24/7 as the fish go around normally in their pens, and avoids any chemical introduction or resistance issues. The reduction in sea lice around the farming area is better for other wild fish populations nearby, too.

Solutions like Stingray do have a few drawbacks. Primarily, fish farming businesses might look sheepishly at the up-front costs of deployment. Moreover, it might be best used as a preventative measure, keeping localized lice populations low. The Stingray’s range is limited now by its deployment in the salmon pens, so lice can gather in darker, murkier corners and outside their patrol area.

#10495. How to Learn Java with AI: A Practical Guide for Beginners

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Java has been one of the most in-demand programming languages for over two decades. It powers Android apps, banking systems, enterprise software, and huge backend platforms. The good news: learning it has never been easier. With AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and GitHub Copilot, you now have a patient tutor available at any hour.

The catch is that AI can help you learn faster or help you avoid learning at all. This guide shows you how to use it the right way.

Traditionally, learning Java meant reading a textbook, watching videos, and getting stuck on a compiler error for two hours with nobody to ask. AI removes much of that friction:

Instant explanations. Ask "what is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?" and get an answer pitched at your level.

Personalized pace. Ask for the same concept explained three different ways until it clicks.

Error decoding. Paste a confusing stack trace and get a plain-English explanation of what went wrong.

Unlimited practice. Generate fresh exercises on any topic, any time.

But AI is a tutor, not a replacement for practice. You still have to write the code yourself.

Before writing code, you need the JDK (Java Development Kit) and an IDE such as IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code.

"I'm a complete beginner on Windows. Walk me through installing the JDK and IntelliJ IDEA, and help me run my first Hello World program."

If something goes wrong (and it often does with PATH variables), paste the exact error message and ask what it means.

Use AI to build understanding with analogies and examples.

"Explain Java loops like I'm a beginner. Give me one real-world analogy, then three short examples that get progressively harder."

Then close the chat and write your own loop from memory. That second step is where learning actually happens.

OOP is where many beginners struggle, and where AI shines as a tutor. Concepts like classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, and abstraction are easier to grasp when you can ask follow-up questions.

"Teach me inheritance in Java using a Vehicle, Car, and Bike example. Then quiz me with 5 questions, one at a time, and wait for my answer before giving feedback."

Asking the AI to quiz you, rather than just explain, turns passive reading into active recall.

Once you've written a program, ask AI to review it. This is one of the most valuable habits you can build.

"Review my Java code. Point out bugs, style issues, and anything that isn't idiomatic. Explain why each suggestion matters, but don't rewrite the whole thing for me."

That last sentence is important. You want feedback and understanding, not a finished solution you copy and paste.

When your code throws a NullPointerException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, resist the urge to say "fix this." Instead, try:

"Here's my code and the error. Don't give me the answer yet. Ask me guiding questions so I can find the bug myself."

Debugging is a core professional skill. Using AI as a Socratic coach builds that skill instead of bypassing it.

Tutorials only take you so far. Projects are where Java sticks. Ask AI to suggest projects matched to your level:

Beginner: Number guessing game, to-do list in the console, simple calculator

Intermediate: Library management system, bank account simulator, student record manager

Advanced: REST API with Spring Boot, inventory system with a database, a chat application

"I know Java basics and OOP. Suggest a project I can finish in a weekend, break it into milestones, and don't write the code for me."

Copy-pasting without understanding. If you can't explain a line of code, you haven't learned it. Ask the AI to explain it line by line.

Trusting AI blindly. AI can produce code that looks right but is wrong, outdated, or insecure. Always run it, test it, and verify against official documentation.

Skipping the struggle. A little frustration is productive. Try for 15 to 20 minutes before asking for help.

Never writing code from scratch. Regularly practice without AI so you know what you can actually do on your own, especially before job interviews.

AI is a fantastic assistant, but it can't tell you what you don't know you need to learn. A structured course gives you a proven roadmap, so you cover the right topics in the right order, while AI fills in the gaps, answers your questions, and keeps you moving.

The best way to learn Java with AI is to treat it like a good mentor: ask it to explain, challenge, and review, but do the typing yourself. Learners who combine consistent practice with smart AI use progress faster than ever before.

#10494. People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

One finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports

"Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

There is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts

The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

To investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

The AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that users associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 users who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize."

The most striking difference involved hunger.

In retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

But among Reddit users who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the new findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

These differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean."

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

In their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

"That's what we hope will happen with this study," says Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing."

The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

#10493. mmBERT: ModernBERT goes Multilingual

This blog post introduces mmBERT, a state-of-the-art massively multilingual encoder model trained on 3T+ tokens of text in over 1800 languages. It shows significant performance and speed improvements over previous multilingual models, being the first to improve upon XLM-R, while also developing new strategies for effectively learning low-resource languages. mmBERT builds upon ModernBERT for a blazingly fast architecture, and adds novel components to enable efficient multilingual learning.

If you are interested in trying out the models yourself, some example boilerplate is available at the end of this blogpost!

mmBERT was trained on a carefully curated multilingual dataset totaling over 3T tokens across three distinct training phases. The foundation of our training data consists of three primary open-source and high-quality web crawls that enable both multilingual coverage and data quality:

DCLM and Filtered DCLM provides the highest quality English content available, serving as the backbone for strong English performance (with the filtered data coming from Dolmino). This dataset represents state-of-the-art web filtering techniques and forms a crucial component. Due to the high quality of this data, we use a signficantly higher proportion of English than previous generation multilingual encoder models (up to 18%).

FineWeb2 delivers broad multilingual web content covering over 1,800 languages. This dataset enables our extensive multilingual coverage while maintaining reasonable quality standards across diverse language families and scripts.

FineWeb2-HQ consists of a filtered subset of FineWeb2 focusing on 20 high-resource languages. This filtered version provides higher-quality multilingual content that bridges the gap between English-only filtered data and broad multilingual coverage.

The training data also incorporates specialized corpora from Dolma, MegaWika v2, ProLong and more: code repositories (StarCoder, ProLong), academic content (ArXiv, PeS2o), reference materials (Wikipedia, textbooks), and community discussions (StackExchange), along with instruction and mathematical datasets.

The key innovation in our data approach is the progressive language inclusion strategy shown in Figure 1. At each phase we progressively sample from a flatter distribution (i.e. closer to uniform), while also adding new languages. This means that high resource languages like Russian start off with a high percentage of the data (i.e. 9%) and then in the last phase of training end around half of that. We start with 60 high-resource languages during pre-training, expand to 110 languages during mid-training, and finally include all 1,833 languages from FineWeb2 during the decay phase. This allows us to maximize the impact of limited low-resource language data without excess reptitions and while maintaining high overall data quality.

mmBERT builds upon the ModernBERT architecture but introduces several key innovations for multilingual learning:

We use the same core architecture as ModernBERT-base with 22 layers and 1152 intermediate dimensions, but switch to the Gemma 2 tokenizer to better handle multilingual text. The base model has 110M non-embedding parameters (307M total due to the larger vocabulary), while the small variant has 42M non-embedding parameters (140M total).

Our training follows a carefully designed three-phase schedule:

Inverse Mask Ratio Schedule: Instead of using a fixed masking rate, we progressively reduce the mask ratio from 30% → 15% → 5% across training phases. This allows the model to learn basic representations with higher masking early on, then focus on more nuanced understanding with lower masking rates.

Annealed Language Learning: We dynamically adjust the temperature for multilingual data sampling from τ=0.7 → 0.5 → 0.3. This creates a progression from high-resource language bias toward more uniform sampling, enabling the model to build a strong multilingual foundation before learning low-resource languages.

Progressive Language Addition: Rather than training on all languages simultaneously, we strategically add languages at each phase (60 → 110 → 1,833). This maximizes learning efficiency by avoiding excessive epochs on limited low-resource data while still achieving strong performance.

Model Merging: We train three different variants during the decay phase (English-focused, 110-language, and all-language) and use TIES merging to combine their strengths into the final model.

English Performance: On the English GLUE benchmark (Table 1), mmBERT base achieves strong performance, substantially outperforming other multilingual models like XLM-R (multilingual RoBERTa) base and mGTE base, while remaining competitive to English-only models despite less than 25% of the mmBERT training data being English.

Multilingual Performance: mmBERT shows significant improvements on XTREME benchmark compared to XLM-R as demonstrated in Table 2. Notable gains include strong performance on XNLI classification, substantial improvements in question answering tasks like TyDiQA, and competitive results across PAWS-X and XCOPA for cross-lingual understanding.

The model performs well across most categories, with the exception of some structured prediction tasks like NER and POS tagging, likely due to tokenizer differences that affect word boundary detection. On these categories, it performs about the same as the previous generation, but can be applied to more languages.

English Retrieval: Even though mmBERT is designed for massively multilingual settings, in the MTEB v2 English benchmarks (Table 3), mmBERT shows significant gains over previous multilingual models and even ties the capabilities of English-only models like ModernBERT!

Multilingual Retrieval: mmBERT shows consistent improvements on MTEB v2 multilingual benchmarks compared to other models (Table 4).

Code Retrieval: Due to the modern tokenizer (based on Gemma 2) mmBERT also shows strong coding performance (Table 5), making mmBERT suitable for any type of textual data. The only model that outperforms it is EuroBERT, which was able to use the non-publicly accessible Stack v2 dataset.

One of mmBERT's most significant novel features is demonstrating that low-resource languages can be effectively learned during the short decay phase of training. We validated this approach by testing on languages only introduced during the final 100B token decay phase.

Dramatic Performance Gains: Testing on TiQuaD (Tigrinya) and FoQA (Faroese), we observed substantial improvements when these languages were included in the decay phase, as shown in Figure 2. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our progressive language learning approach.

Competitive with Large Models: Despite only seeing these languages in the final training phase, mmBERT achieves performance levels that exceed much larger models. On Faroese question answering where LLMs have been benchmarked, mmBERT outperforms Google Gemini 2.5 Pro and OpenAI o3.

Rapid Learning Mechanism: The success of decay-phase language learning stems from the model's ability to leverage its strong multilingual foundation built during earlier phases. When exposed to new languages, the model can quickly adapt existing cross-lingual representations rather than learning from scratch.

Model Merging Benefits: The final mmBERT models successfully retain most of the decay-phase improvements while benefiting from the English-focused and high-resource variants through TIES merging.

mmBERT delivers substantial efficiency gains over previous multilingual encoder models through architectural improvements inherited from ModernBERT:

Throughput Performance: mmBERT processes text significantly faster than existing multilingual models across various sequence lengths, as demonstrated in Figure 3. Both the small and base models show substantial speed improvements over previous multilingual encoders.

Modern Architecture Benefits: The efficiency gains come from two main technical improvements:

Sequence Length Scaling: Unlike older models limited to 512 tokens, mmBERT handles up to 8,192 tokens efficiently while maintaining high throughput. This makes it suitable for longer document processing tasks that are increasingly common in multilingual applications.

Energy Efficiency: The combination of better throughput and modern architecture results in lower computational costs for inference, making mmBERT more practical for production deployments where multilingual support is needed at scale.

These efficiency improvements make mmBERT not just more accurate than previous multilingual encoders, but also significantly more practical for real usage.

You can use these models with just a few lines of code!

can someone point me to how can i use the mmBERT model for BERTscore , a translation eval metric

Hi @StephennFernandes ! It's been a while since I used BERTScore, but wherever you see another BERT model (or XLM-R or similar) feel free to replace the model name with mmBERT. I would suggest checking out https://github.com/Tiiiger/bert_score for more details and perhaps raising an issue there if it's unclear.

#10492. MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "

A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot

The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."

To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

#10490. Jupyter Agents: training LLMs to reason with notebooks

The past year has been all about giving LLMs more tools and autonomy to solve more complex and open ended tasks. The goal of the Jupyter Agent is to give the model the ultimate tool: code execution.

A natural way to display multi-step code execution together with reasoning is within a Jupyter Notebook, which consists of code and markdown cells. So we built Jupyter Agent to act as an agent that can execute code directly inside a Jupyter notebook and use this environment to solve data analysis and data science tasks. Think of it like Cursor, but living natively inside your data science workflow.We built a demo of this vision with Qwen-3 Coder, currently one of the strongest coding models. This is a follow-up to our earlier work on jupyter-agent (v1).

While large models are starting to show useful behavior, the key question is how we can continue improving them. To this end, we focus on strengthening smaller models to perform well on agentic data science tasks as they currently struggle to compete with the large models.

The goal of this project is to build a pipeline to first generate high-quality training data, then fine-tune an existing small model, and finally evaluate whether the model's performance improves on relevant benchmarks.

Let’s begin with the last step: selecting a strong benchmark for evaluating models on data science tasks.

In order to understand if we are making progress towards better data science agents we need a benchmark to measure such capabilities. Last year, in partnership with Adyen, we introduced the DABStep benchmark: a way to evaluate data science agents on realistic tasks. The setup is simple: provide the LLM with datasets and ask it to answer non-trivial data questions.

This benchmark remains challenging for today’s LLMs — e.g. the best out-of-the-box model is Claude 4 Sonnet which reaches not even 20% accuracy on the hard tasks.You can explore the live leaderboard here.

Now that we identified a good benchmark we can try to climb it! We set out to build a dataset for fine-tuning such that even a small data agent model could perform well on DABStep.

Our first choice was Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507: extremely small (fast to iterate with, easy to run), yet strong enough to act in agentic scenarios.

Not great — but a promising starting point, since it left a lot of room for improvement. Let's see how we can improve it!

A core aspect of agents that sets it apart from a pure chat model is the scaffolding built around the model to steer its behaviour. The evaluation script in DABStep for example uses smolagents to execute code. Smolagents comes with predefined behaviors, prompting structures, and expected formats.

We also studied the Qwen-Agent codebase, where the authors tailoring scaffolding to the model. This makes sense: Claude Code, for example, works shockingly well with Claude Sonnet because their scaffolding is aligned.

Results: accuracy jumped from 44.4% → 59.7% (easy split). 🚀

With simplified scaffolding in place, we focused on fine-tuning Qwen3-4B for data science agentic tasks.

The recipe to improve a model on a certain task or behaviour is to train it on data that reflects the tasks as closely as possible. A natural starting point is to look at real Jupyter Notebooks and find notebooks that align closely with the task that we plan to tackle, namely data analysis.

Kaggle notebooks offer a wealth of high quality data analysis notebooks and are made available by Kaggle:

Now that we have good results with a base model it's time to build a dataset that will help us improve it even further. We designed a multi-stage pipeline using Datatrove to clean and prepare Kaggle notebooks at scale.

We started with ~2TB of Kaggle notebooks and reduced it to ~250GB reusing our work from the BigCode project. As part of the StarCoder2 training data processing the notebooks (without output cells) were already deduplicated. Most Kaggle notebooks are small variations or near-identical copies, so this step was essential.Key insight: ~90% of raw notebooks are duplicates, which would have skewed training if left unfiltered.

Most Kaggle notebooks reference external datasets via Kaggle metadata. To make sure the code inside notebooks could actually run, we built a pipeline that automatically fetched these linked datasets. This step was crucial, since many notebooks would otherwise be incomplete or non-executable.

Using the kagglehub package, we downloaded thousands of datasets — about 5TB in total. To keep things manageable and relevant:

By the end, we had a rich collection of executable notebooks paired with their datasets, providing the foundation for training agents in realistic, runnable environments.

We scored notebooks based on educational quality using Qwen3-32B. We saw that using the whole notebook was not optimal, as many contained trivial or broken code. Our educational scoring approach is detailed in edu_scoring.py.

TL;DR: We assigned each notebook a score from 1–5 based on clarity, completeness, and educational value, and kept only those above a chosen threshold. This filtering removed about 70% of the notebooks.

This is similar to the insight from the BeyondWeb paper, which showed that using high-quality data is better for synthetic data generation — a step we relied on for QA (Question-Answer) generation. This helped the model learn from “high quality” notebooks instead of noisy ones.

We excluded notebooks about training LLMs or unrelated to data analysis. We also removed notebooks that didn’t actually use datasets through an automated LLM-based filtering process using Qwen3-32B. The implementation of filtering can be found in extract_packages_and_files.py.

TL;DR: We prompted Qwen3-32B to identify and remove notebooks that either (1) had nothing to do with data analysis, or (2) didn’t actually use datasets. This step removed about 20% of the notebooks.

This ensured we trained only on relevant data science tasks.

Using the cleaned notebooks, we generated question–answer pairs using Qwen3-32B. The questions and answer are grounded in the real notebook traces so the QA pairs are based on real code execution results. Prompt design: we asked the LLM to produce natural questions that could realistically be asked of the dataset, then validated whether the notebook provided a correct answer.

Challenge: We had to try many prompts to get higher-difficulty questions because LLMs tended to generate trivial ones like "what is the size of the dataset".Insight: We broke this into two steps because LLMs tended to hallucinate answers:

The complete prompting strategy and implementation is available in generate_qa.py.

Finally we want to generate clean code execution traces since even the original notebooks after processing are often open ended and verbose with lots of irrelevant parts. However, we want our Jupyter Agent to get to the result efficiently. To generate cleaner notebook traces for training we generated traces synthetically based on the original notebooks.We have prompted Qwen-3-Coder-480B model to generate a jupyter notebook code to answer the question from the previously generated synthetic QA pair. Traces captured step-by-step code execution, including intermediate outputs, which are crucial for agent training.

We used E2B for our agent to solve the synthetic QA pairs, which required fetching Kaggle datasets so the code could actually run via E2B.

Challenge 1: Many datasets were unavailable.Trick: Since LLMs are strong at code and have a decent world model, we prompted them to act as a code interpreter when the dataset was missing.

Challenge 2: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B model does not support thinking mode - how can we extract code commentary? By default it often outputs just a brief comment followed by several steps of code execution. However, we'd like some reasoning or comments between every cell. Trick: When switching from Qwen3-32B to Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B we noticed that often output message content was empty. This turns out to be a previously known quirk of Qwen3-Coder models in which when using tool calling the model would not return an empty assistant response. We enforce some text commentary through tooling by passing 'comment' as a required field in the code execution tool call. This way when non-reasoning model is used for code cell generation it will by default output some description of its actions from 1st POV, emulating the thinking traces structure.

Note: the generated final answer in the notebook may vary from the answer specified in the QA pair. This is caused by the fact that the agent model could use data preprocessing methods and steps different from the original Kaggle notebook and the synthetic question would not usually specify them. This discrepancy is normal and lays the foundation for a new exciting research direction of how language models tend to treat data analysis and whether they do it differently from humans. For full transparency we keep both LLM-generated final answer and original answer from the real Kaggle notebook as a signal of model's performance. We encourage the community to try different dataset mixes to see how they can push performance even further.

We truncated overly long outputs and filtered out trivial traces to prevent content length issues and keep only high-quality traces.We kept non-trivial, multi-turn traces aligned with DABStep-style tasks.The resulting Jupyter Agent Dataset became the foundation for SFT on Qwen3-4B models with 51k synthetic notebooks and almost 0.2B tokens.

With the curated dataset ready, we turned to the key question: does this data actually help the model get better at solving data analysis tasks? To find out, we set up a simple fine-tuning pipeline and ran experiments to measure the impact of training on our synthetic notebooks.

We observe that it is beneficial to have a bit more epochs than usual for SFT with lower learning rate and higher neftune noise (7). In summary, we can see up to 36%/22% boost on DABStep easy score compared with base/scaffolded model:

We can also see, that the hard score can increase too even though our dataset is focused on easier questions:

In practice, the model can now solve a wide range of realistic Kaggle-style data analysis tasks with consistent execution.It’s not yet strong enough for the hardest queries, but we’ve shown that even small models can become powerful agents when paired with the right data and scaffolding.

These results demonstrate that even small models can become powerful data science agents with the right training approach. Ready to try it yourself? We've made everything openly available so you can experiment with our fine-tuned models and dataset.

This modder thought opening a window was too much work, so he did something cool about it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

u/Motor_Attention1865 on Reddit didn't like how his PC added extra heat to his room in the winter, so he went the extra mile to dump the heat outside in a fashion similar to mini-split air conditioners. The external cooling system is controlled by an Arduino Mega that the PC communicates with when it needs extra cooling. The system opens a three-way valve to route coolant outside and prevents condensation by keeping the coolant temperature above the dew point.

Our intrepid modder's room has heated floors, and the PC was dumping too much heat under the table where his PC sits, even in 25 °F (-4 °C) weather. He grew tired of manually opening a window to regulate the temperature in his space, so he put in much more effort to create a split cooling system that puts another radiator outside in the below-freezing temperatures, cooling down the PC significantly.

Motor_Attention1865's build itself is impressive enough, with a delidded Core Ultra 7 270K Plus cooled by a Thermal Grizzly 1851 Mycro Pro direct-die water block with Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut Extreme liquid compound. Not only is his RTX 4070 Ti Super also watercooled with a Bykski water block, but the 2x24GB DDR5-8400 G.Skill RAM is also watercooled using Bykski heat spreaders with an IceManCooler two-channel water block. The cooling system within the PC has two radiators: a 120mm in the back and a 360mm in the front, all fed by an EK Kinetic D5 pump-reservoir.

The external cooling system, however, is even more impressive. The 240mm outdoor radiator with two Noctua iPPC-3000 fans isn’t outrageous, but the automated system that makes it useful is what’s interesting. Next to the PC is a box with a Bykski D5 pump and reservoir that pushes water outside, but it doesn’t use the external radiator until the PC needs the extra cooling.

Upon startup, the PC runs a Python script that communicates with an Arduino Mega connected to three temperature probes checking the coolant temperature and three more temperature and humidity sensors that monitor the PC case and the ambient air. The sensors give the Arduino Mega information on where to switch the motorized three-way valve depending on the temperature and humidity.

The problem with extreme cold in any PC is condensation. If coolant gets below the dew point of the environment, condensation forms, potentially shorting out PC components. To prevent this disaster, the Arduino determines the dew point based on the humidity and temperature of the room and in the PC. Motor_Attention1865 set the Arduino to close off the outside radiator at +10 °C above the dew point, or +5 °C during benchmarking, allowing for low temperatures without risking droplets forming in the PC.

Because of the freezing or below-freezing temperatures at which this external loop is meant to operate, Motor_Attention1865 also added pure ethylene glycol to the Aquacomputer Double Protect Ultra Clear coolant in the loop, lowering its freezing point from -18 °C to -28 °C.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Thanks to the supplemental cooling system and delidding, the system achieves temperatures below 50 °C under heavy use. According to Motor_Attention1865, the RTX 4070 Ti sits at 37 °C and the CPU hovers around 45-50 °C while gaming. Temperatures were higher in benchmarks, however — in Cinebench R23, the CPU sat at 52 °C, while in 3DMark Steel Nomad, the GPU was at 48 °C.

Above all, however, Motor_Attention1865 no longer needs to bother himself with opening a window if their room gets too hot with the PC under load. It's the small things.
