#10389. Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia won’t end his problems with Congress

Jensen Huang may be out at Nvidia, but the questions surrounding his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy—and what it might have meant for American national security—are only growing more serious.

The billionaire’s resignation Thursday has done little to quiet a scandal that threatens to reach well beyond Nvidia’s boardroom, raising questions about the Trump administration’s controversial decisions to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China. Huang played an influential role in shaping those policies. Now, Congress wants to know whether his personal relationship with a Chinese businesswoman exposed sensitive American technology or national security information to Beijing—and what government officials knew about the potential risks.

Despite his departure as Nvidia’s chairman and CEO, Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before congressional investigators. The former CEO and lawmakers have been discussing the timing of the closed-door hearing, which could provide answers about his relationship with an executive at a company suspected of funneling restricted Nvidia chips to Chinese AI labs.

Three Republican committee chairs in the House of Representatives—Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—requested Huang’s testimony in a November 4 letter, more than a week before his resignation. Mast told reporters Thursday that his committee still wanted to speak to Huang, adding that his staff had been in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night. Later that day, Bloomberg and NBC News reported that Huang had agreed to appear without a subpoena.

The request followed an October 29 New York Times investigation into Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a company U.S. intelligence had suspected for more than a year of collaborating with the Chinese government and helping funnel trade-restricted AI chips to Chinese labs. The lawmakers are concerned that Alice Huang may also have provided Beijing with access to trade secrets and sensitive national security information.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s (People’s Republic of China) access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

Trump could be implicated, too

But the congressional scrutiny is no longer limited to Huang or Nvidia. Lawmakers are increasingly asking whether the Trump administration overlooked warnings about potential Chinese espionage while allowing the company to expand sales of advanced AI chips to China.

On November 11, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller demanding that the administration preserve documents concerning Nvidia’s chip exports, the suspected intelligence operation, and government investigations into Megaspeed.

The senators specifically requested records concerning an intelligence memorandum reportedly circulated to senior administration officials ahead of Trump’s May 2026 visit to China. They also sought communications between Huang and Trump, records of discussions about chip export restrictions, and documents concerning the government’s handling of its investigation into Megaspeed. The question, at the core of their inquiry, is whether national security concerns were sidelined as Huang and the Trump administration pursued policies that benefited Nvidia.

Huang has been one of the tech industry’s most prominent supporters of Donald Trump. Nvidia contributed $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and $25 million toward the White House ballroom now under construction. Huang himself has visited Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida and the White House numerous times, and has traveled with the president.

His influence on U.S. export policy regarding AI chips is evident. He’s credited with persuading the Trump administration to allow sales of Nvidia H20 and H200 chips to China. Huang argued that letting the chips, and the CUDA software framework that runs them, proliferate around the world was good for America. Nvidia also agreed to pay the U.S. government 15% of revenue from H20 sales and 25% from H200 sales.

Nvidia defended the arrangement last December. “The Administration’s licensing process will ensure that sales of H200 to authorized customers worldwide do not deprive U.S. customers of anything—and will in fact benefit American national and economic security,” spokesman John Rizzo said in a statement to Fast Company. “Offering H200 to approved and known commercial customers, vetted by the Department of Commerce, raises no cybersecurity risk and strikes a thoughtful balance that is great for America.”

Those assurances now face renewed scrutiny. Megaspeed bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips in recent years, including some of its most powerful Blackwell chips, which remain off limits to Chinese labs. A New York Times report last year described finding boxes of powerful Nvidia chips at a nearly empty Megaspeed office in Malaysia, raising suspicions that the company was serving as a conduit for restricted technology bound for China.

There are also unanswered questions about the government’s response. The Commerce Department opened an investigation into Megaspeed last year, but the inquiry was subsequently transferred to the Department of Justice, with little publicly known about what happened afterward. The Warren–Coons letter seeks records that could help establish what senior Trump administration officials knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, why the White House and the Commerce Department allowed chip shipments to Megaspeed to continue, and whether or not the White House disregarded national security recommendations to accommodate Nvidia’s commercial interests.

These questions could become more consequential when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Coons, who is expected to chair the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has also called for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia to determine whether national security was compromised while Nvidia and the White House benefited financially from chip sales to China.

“We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration,” Coons wrote on X.

For Nvidia, meanwhile, the immediate consequences have been severe. Its shares have lost nearly a quarter of their value—24.6%—since The New York Times first reported on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang on October 29.

Nvidia has not publicly offered a detailed explanation for accepting Huang’s resignation. Its SEC filing simply states that the board accepted his departure. But the decision may have had less to do with the morality of Huang’s personal conduct than with the growing financial and political risks of keeping him in charge.

SpaceX/xAI is developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system that replaces conventional NVLink cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board (PCB), in part for use in orbital data centers, reports SemiAnalysis. The system is codenamed Kessel and retains 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, but introduces a different solid-state interconnect architecture. While SpaceX/xAI will continue to buy Nvidia hardware directly from the company, Elon Musk's company will source other components independently, which could give it greater control over its hardware supply chain.

The Kessel system retains the fundamental configuration of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which comprises 72 GPU packages distributed across 18 compute trays and nine NVLink switch trays. However, instead of Nvidia's conventional arrangement with internal NVLink cable cartridges, SpaceX plans to position compute and switch trays back-to-back around a passive PCB midplane. The architecture resembles a smaller version of Nvidia's Kyber design with 576 AI GPUs (albeit in 144 packages), which also relies on a PCB-based interconnect rather than conventional cable assemblies, SemiAnalysis notes. Interestingly, the design is aimed at both terrestrial and orbital deployments, according to the analysts.

Arguably the most distinctive feature of Kessel is its 84-layer PCB midplane, which uses ultra-low-loss M10 copper-clad laminates (CCLs). By contrast, Nvidia's Kyber architecture relied on a backplane based on a considerably more complex 156-layer PCB featuring M9 CCLs. The reduction in layer count by nearly half could substantially improve manufacturability and production yields, but the more advanced copper-clad laminate will almost certainly increase material costs. In any case, an 84-layer PCB is a device that is exceptionally hard to build.

The move to a PCB midplane could simplify system assembly by eliminating numerous high-speed cable connections, but it would not necessarily reduce manufacturing costs. An 84-layer PCB that relies on ultra-low-loss M10 laminate is an exceptionally expensive component that requires sophisticated manufacturing processes and precise quality control. To put an 84-layer PCB number into context, modern high-end server motherboards use 15 – 20 layers, whereas server development boards use more than 20 layers to virtually eliminate any electrical issues with the board itself. Furthermore, manufacturing yields of an 84-layer PCB could become a major obstacle, as defects in internal layers may render an entire board unusable. Consequently, the economic viability of Kessel will depend on whether savings from cable elimination and independent component procurement can offset the cost of its complex midplane.

Perhaps more importantly, Kessel represents a departure from Nvidia's conventional system-level procurement model. Instead of purchasing Nvidia's assembled L6 compute boards or even L10 trays that Nvidia plans to sell with its Vera Rubin generation, SpaceX reportedly plans to acquire AI accelerators, CPUs, switches, and networking components directly from Nvidia and procure other components from third-party suppliers (one can wonder how easy it will be for SpaceX/xAI to procure memory amid today's shortages). This would enable SpaceX to select its own PCB manufacturers, component vendors, and manufacturing partners, optimize its hardware for its infrastructure (which will be important for orbital deployments), and perhaps reduce intermediary costs. Meanwhile, the company would assume greater responsibility for system design, validation, manufacturing quality, and supply-chain management, which is something that most hyperscalers have been doing in recent years.

For Nvidia, the implications are less straightforward. Although direct sales of CPU and AI GPU packages could reduce the company's revenue from complete compute-board assemblies, the arrangement could also encourage other large customers to develop their own Nvidia-based systems and eventually deploy more Nvidia-based machines, something that may be important in a world where custom silicon developed by hyperscalers is rapidly gaining traction. However, to make this happen, Kessel must be a smashing success that will offer clear advantages over systems designed by Nvidia.

#10386. Whipped cream sold at Costco is being recalled because it could have cleaning chemicals inside

Thanksgiving is less than two weeks away, which means millions of Americans will soon be sitting down to pumpkin and pecan pies topped with healthy doses of whipped cream.

But now a popular whipped cream product sold at Costco is being recalled over fears that it could be contaminated with cleaning chemicals. Here’s what you need to know.

What happened?

Discount wholesale giant Costco announced a recall of one of its whipped cream products sold under the company’s Kirkland Signature brand. The alert was posted on Costco’s recalls website with a November 7 notice from Alamance Foods.

Alamance Foods specializes in manufacturing dairy creams and foams as well as beverages and other products for retailers and grocery chains’ private-label brands.

For Costco, Alamance Foods manufactures select Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream products.

The recall is voluntary, the notice states, and is being done “out of an abundance of caution” after it was found that the product “may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical.”

What Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream product is being recalled?

According to the recall notice, one type of Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream product is being recalled:

  • Product: Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream, 15 oz (425 g), case pack 8CT/3PK, item code AC50
  • Lot: 04/02/2027 (Best If Used By APR/02/27)
  • Timestamps affected on can: 00:35 – 02:45

Images of the recalled product’s packaging are available in the recall notice here.

Where was the recalled product sold?

According to the notice, the recalled whipped cream product was sold in the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Florida
  • Georgia
  • Iowa
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Missouri
  • Mississippi
  • North Carolina
  • South Carolina
  • Tennessee
  • Wisconsin

Has anyone been harmed by the recalled whipped cream?

Thankfully, there are no reports of illness or other harm to consumers who have purchased the now-recalled whipped cream. 

“Members have reported a chemical smell and taste, but no serious adverse effects requiring medical care have been reported,” the November 7 recall notice states.

What should I do if I have the recalled whipped cream?

Do not consume it. Instead, the recall notice states you should stop using it and instead return the item to Costco for a full refund.

Consumers with questions about the recall can contact Alamance Foods at customer.care@alamancefood.com.

#10384. Top 6 AI YouTube Transcript Generators: Features, Accuracy, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

There is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Is it legal to transcribe someone else's YouTube video? Transcribing for personal research or accessibility is common, but republishing the text may infringe copyright. Check the video's license and YouTube's terms, and get permission when in doubt.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#10382. Pharmaceutical ads may influence which drug AI recommends, new research finds

Next time you ask AI for medical advice, you may want to consider whether it’s been influenced by Big Pharma. Prescription drug advertisements are everywhere and may affect AI’s recommendations, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health this week.

The study authors conducted experiments with a dozen consumer-facing large language models (LLMs), including versions of Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT—made by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, respectively. 

Clinical guidance or commercial influence?

The models were tested across 33 scenarios that each included a clinical case description and multiple treatment options. In some cases, the AI models were also given an ad for one of the treatment options. The ad’s content included information about the drug and its uses, but did not specifically direct the AI model to recommend the drug.

When exposed to an ad, AI models recommended the treatment in question an average of 47.6% of the time, compared with 35% when no ad was present. However, the size of these shifts varied among the 12 models.

Although the models often changed their recommendation when an ad was present, in most cases they still selected one of the appropriate options. The outputs only disclosed the ad’s presence about 30% of the time. 

“An answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise an important question about why the AI arrived at that answer,” study author Dr. Girish Nadkarni, a professor of medicine and system chair of the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine, said in a statement. “As AI becomes part of how people get health information, we need to be able to distinguish clinical guidance from commercial influence and be transparent about when advertising is part of the interaction.”

Pharmaceutical companies spent more than $6 billion on TV advertising alone in 2024, according to a report by the pharmaceutical data, analytics, and consulting firm IQVIA, which said that direct-to-consumer advertising “directly influences patient requests and prescription rates, driving real action in healthcare.”

Most countries ban drug ads

All high-income countries, save for the U.S. and New Zealand, ban direct-to-consumer ads for prescription drugs.

In the U.S., prescription drugs consume more than 30% of commercial time during major networks’ evening news programs, according to a 2025 press release from the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

Last year, ranking member Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the End Prescription Drug Ads Now Act, co-signed by six other senators, which would ban such advertising, including on social media. 

In practice, the Lancet study said, AI models could be exposed to drug ads “through user prompts, application-added context, retrieved online material, or inadvertent or malicious insertion,” and that, “unlike television or print advertising, which is subject to U.S. Food and Drug Administration oversight, AI-mediated promotion might not fit existing categories.” 

However, the study did not examine whether these measured effects translate into real-world changes in patient requests or prescriptions.

The chatbot will see you now

In a recent Doximity survey of 3,379 U.S. physicians, 54% said they had moderate or high levels of trust in AI’s ability to recommend treatment or management. Three-quarters of respondents also said patients had become more likely to propose a diagnosis or treatment plan suggested by AI over the past six months. 

“Clinicians might defer to algorithmic recommendations even when they conflict with clinical judgment,” the study’s authors said, and an appropriate but ad-influenced suggestion “might provide little reason to question it.”

As GTA 6, the most anticipated game of the year, perhaps the decade, nears its November 19 release date, one company has offered its employees the chance to take the day off to play it. Amid the expectation that gamers around the globe will call in sick to play the game instead of heading into the office, PC peripheral and hardware outfit Logitech is getting ahead of the game by giving 7,000 employees the chance to take a day off to play it. As for Logitech, the company believes that it's time for people to move away from the belief that playing games is a waste of time, hence its new initiative. It makes sense for a company that makes gaming accessories to say that, of course, but CEO Hanneke Faber argues that the company sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.” The hope will be that, by allowing employees to play games, a productivity boost will follow.

Whether that comes to fruition remains to be seen. But there's less doubt about GTA 6's popularity a little more than a week out from its release. If you've yet to get your order in, you can also grab Grand Theft Auto VI for $79.99 now. #10379. The untapped potential of a smarter SPIFF strategy

Manufacturers invest a lot in getting their products into the right channels. But once those products reach a dealer network, the brand gives up a significant amount of control over what happens next.

Suddenly, someone outside your organization is responsible for understanding your products, remembering what differentiates them, and recommending them when the right customer walks through the door.

And they may be doing the same thing for dozens of competing brands.

That’s one reason sales performance incentive funds (SPIFFs) have become such a familiar tool. Give retail sales associates a financial incentive to sell a particular product, and you create an immediate reason to prioritize it.

But an incentive alone can only do so much. The bigger opportunity is using the SPIFF to engage dealers more consistently. It can help you build a strategy around the program that reinforces your brand remaining relevant long after the initial announcement.

THE INCENTIVE AS PART OF THE EXPERIENCE

It’s easy to think about a SPIFF primarily in terms of the offer: How much will participants earn? Which products qualify? How long will the promotion run? But also consider why someone would continue paying attention to the program. And consider the experience from the dealer’s perspective.

You’ll want to ensure the program is clearly explained and that registration is easy. Make it very obvious which products qualify and why they are worth recommending. Include a list of useful selling points to use while talking to customers. And ask yourself whether they are being reminded about the opportunity after the program launch.

A SPIFF can have an attractive incentive and still underperform if it isn’t reinforced after launch or the experience around it creates friction. The strongest programs address motivation and engagement.

PRODUCT EDUCATION

A financial reward gives someone a reason to make a sale, but product knowledge helps them make that sale confidently.

Retail sales associates often recommend products among multiple brands that can meet a customer’s needs. If your brand wants to earn the recommendation, the person making it needs to understand why your product is relevant to the customer standing in front of them.

Customers want to know what makes your product different. They’re looking for relevant benefits that matter to them along with proof points to back up the recommendation. And it helps to know which products are right for which customers.

A SPIFF creates a natural opportunity to reinforce those issues. Product education should be built into the communications surrounding it. Use the program to continually give dealers useful information they can apply on the sales floor.

Over time, that familiarity can build something even more valuable: brand preference. When sales associates understand your products and appreciate what makes them different, they will feel confident recommending them. They can become genuine advocates for your brand. And in a competitive retail environment, having an informed, enthusiastic advocate on the sales floor can be a powerful differentiator.

MAINTAIN THE PROGRAM AFTER LAUNCH

Many marketing initiatives receive their greatest communications push at the beginning. There’s the launch email. The sales materials. The landing page. Maybe a kickoff meeting or announcement. Then attention moves elsewhere.

The problem is that your dealers’ attention moves elsewhere, too. Sustained participation requires sustained visibility. You need to create a communications cadence that gives people reasons to keep paying attention.

Remind them about the opportunity and highlight featured products. Reinforce key selling points and share program updates. Give internal sales teams tools to continue the conversation. Use consumer-facing marketing to help create demand that supports what dealers are being asked to sell.

Each touchpoint can reinforce the others. That’s when a collection of promotional tactics starts becoming an integrated dealer engagement strategy.

THINK BEYOND THE SPIFF

The larger lesson extends beyond any single incentive program. Manufacturers that sell through dealers depend on people outside their organizations to represent their brands every day. Yet dealer engagement can easily become transactional. To combat this, communicate when there’s a new product or promotion, or something else the dealer can focus on.

There’s an opportunity to think more broadly.

The goal is to make your brand easier to understand, easier to sell, and easier to remember. That means giving dealers the information they need to better serve their customers. Manufacturers should ensure that sales and marketing efforts reinforce one another, and use it to consistently build familiarity and confidence that make your brand the one they genuinely prefer to recommend.

A SPIFF can provide an ideal moment to put those principles into practice. By making the experience more engaging, educational, and valuable for retail sales associates, manufacturers have an opportunity to build stronger brand relationships.

Manufacturers can potentially turn occasional sellers into enthusiastic brand ambassadors. Because when a sales associate has a genuine preference for your brand, that connection can influence recommendations long after the incentive ends.

Chris K. Bailey is president and CEO of Bailey Brand Consulting.

#10377. Nintendo Switch 2 emulation on Android already has The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake up and running

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

The user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

#10376. OpenAI board member makes a terrifying prediction: You will probably die from an AI accident

Anxieties around an AI doomsday have been ramping up for months, and executives at top AI companies have done little to ease those worries. OpenAI’s Sam Altman said humanity could lose control of the technology. Anthropic warned that its models could be abused to create chemical weapons.

But no AI leaders have looked people dead in the eye and said they specifically are going to be killed by artificial intelligence—until now.

Enter Paul Christiano, an OpenAI board member serving on its Safety and Security Committee. Earlier this week while speaking at the AI Safety Foundation’s annual Hinton Lectures, Christiano said he believes an AI takeover is imminent and that it spells certain doom for the human race.

“For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” Christiano told the crowd.

What does an AI takeover mean to Christiano? He described it as “a situation where there are AI systems pursuing goals, and those systems call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth.”

“If, say, you or me or Donald Trump wanted to stop them, [we] would be as ineffective as if you or me were trying to stop the U.S. military,” he added.

Christiano’s AI timeline

How soon could humanity’s AI downfall happen? Christiano predicts it could occur within the next six months, or—somewhat more reassuringly?—take up to three years.

“If we tried to develop AI along the most rapid trajectory, if we said we’re just going to build this as quickly as we can in the easiest way we can, we would be looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” he reasoned.

On the bright side, Christiano said companies are avoiding that coin flip by pacing the frontier, as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recommended after a former employee accused both Anthropic and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives.”

However, Christiano warns that “even with realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high.”

If anything, his outlook has grown slightly more urgent since joining OpenAI’s board in September. At the time, he estimated a 4% chance of losing control of AI within a year—double the six-month minimum he floated this week—and a 15% chance within three years (odds he acknowledged are based on his subjective beliefs).

“If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment, I expect we will permanently lose control of it,” Christiano wrote in a personal statement. “If that happens then most people could die. I believe we would need domestic and international coordination to ensure global consistency and reduce risk to an acceptable level.”

#10374. Best Static Website Hosting Providers in 2027: Free and Paid Options Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free plans, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

The harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

That doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

There are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

Free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby plan to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

You can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

Generous free plan for typical static websites.

Monthly build limits can matter for frequently updated projects.

Cloudflare's product range can make the initial setup less straightforward for beginners.

Cloudflare is increasingly emphasizing Workers Static Assets for new projects. Pages remains available, but developers starting a new application should compare both deployment approaches.

For a conventional static website, however, Pages is still a practical option, particularly when traffic could grow beyond the limits of other free plans.

See the official Cloudflare Pages limits for the current allowances.

Netlify combines static website hosting with tools designed to make development and deployment easier.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a new version whenever you push changes.

It also creates deploy previews, allowing you to inspect changes before merging them into your production branch.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

Netlify supports custom domains, HTTPS, serverless functions, and form handling.

Netlify's free plan uses a credit-based model with 300 credits per month.

Production deployments consume 15 credits each.

Web requests consume 2 credits per 10,000 requests.

Deploy previews and branch deployments consume no deployment credits.

The paid Personal plan starts at $9 per month and includes 1,000 monthly credits.

Convenient Git integration and deploy previews.

Built-in features such as forms and serverless functions.

Suitable for both simple websites and more advanced front-end projects.

Credit-based pricing requires monitoring several types of usage.

A busy site with frequent deployments can consume its free allowance faster than expected.

When comparing Netlify alternatives, Cloudflare Pages is particularly worth considering if your main concern is bandwidth.

For developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

Vercel also supports server-side rendering, functions, and other features beyond traditional static site hosting.

There is one important restriction: Vercel Hobby is intended for personal, non-commercial use only.

If you're deploying a business website or another commercial project, you'll need an appropriate paid plan.

Convenient deployment workflow for Next.js.

Supports both static and server-rendered applications.

Paid usage can involve multiple resource-based charges.

If you're building a personal Next.js application, Vercel is an obvious candidate. For a basic HTML website, however, its additional framework features may be unnecessary.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

Published websites have a maximum size of 1 GB.

Bandwidth has a soft limit of 100 GB per month.

Free accounts can publish Pages sites from public repositories.

The bandwidth and build restrictions are soft limits, meaning they aren't necessarily enforced as strict cutoffs.

Simple integration with GitHub repositories.

Well suited to documentation and open-source projects.

Free accounts require a public repository for Pages.

GitHub Pages is not intended for running online businesses, e-commerce websites, or commercial SaaS products.

GitHub Pages is particularly convenient if your code already lives on GitHub and you only need to publish documentation or a portfolio.

For commercial websites, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify may be more appropriate.

The GitHub Pages documentation explains its hosting limits and usage restrictions.

Not every website needs a repository, deployment pipeline, or command-line interface.

If you've created a simple HTML page and want to share it, TiinyHost lets you upload an HTML file or ZIP archive and publish it under a shareable URL.

It can also host PDFs, making it useful for sharing documents and presentations alongside website projects.

The main advantage is the upload process. You don't need to configure a repository or install development tools before publishing.

Sharing an HTML file with someone who doesn't use Git.

The free plan includes one active site, a 3 MB project upload limit, and an allowance of 5,000 monthly visits.

The Tiny plan costs €5 per month when billed monthly. It supports uploads up to 25 MB and includes built-in analytics.

The Solo plan starts at €13 per month when billed monthly and adds features such as custom domains, password protection, and additional projects.

Annual billing is available at lower effective monthly prices.

No Git repository or command line required.

Suitable for previews and smaller projects.

The free plan's 3 MB limit is restrictive for websites with many images or other assets.

Custom domains require the Solo plan or higher.

Upload-based publishing is less convenient than Git automation for frequently updated websites.

For someone who simply needs free HTML hosting to share a small project, TiinyHost is worth considering.

For a larger production website that receives regular updates, Git-based hosting is likely to be more manageable.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

That makes it useful when a website needs static hosting but also relies on Google's back-end services.

Deployment is handled through the Firebase command-line interface.

After configuring your project, you can deploy using:

Firebase distributes website assets through its CDN and supports custom domains with SSL certificates.

The Blaze plan uses pay-as-you-go billing while retaining applicable no-cost allowances.

One detail worth checking is the distinction between Firebase Hosting and Firebase App Hosting. They are separate products with different features and pricing models.

Integrates with Firebase Authentication and Firestore.

Useful for applications already using Google's developer services.

Initial setup is more involved than uploading an HTML file.

The daily transfer allowance may become restrictive for larger websites.

Firebase Hosting makes the most sense when Firebase is already part of your application.

For a standalone static blog or portfolio that doesn't use Firebase services, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages may be simpler.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Free allowances may apply depending on your account and the current AWS pricing program, but you should calculate costs based on your expected traffic, storage, and requests.

Unlike simpler hosting services, there isn't one fixed monthly price for every website.

Several services can contribute to the final bill.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common issue when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

The service includes CDN delivery, custom domains, and managed TLS certificates.

Render is particularly useful when your project includes both a static front end and back-end services that you want to manage through the same platform.

Render's Hobby workspace is free and includes:

500 standard build pipeline minutes per month.

Additional bandwidth is billed at $0.15 per GB under the current pricing structure, so the Hobby workspace should not be treated as unlimited free hosting.

The Pro workspace costs $25 per month, excluding any applicable usage-based compute charges.

Static websites and back-end services on one platform.

The 5 GB included bandwidth allowance is relatively small.

Render makes sense when you're already using it for other parts of an application.

If you only need to host a static HTML website, Cloudflare Pages offers a more generous bandwidth allowance without the additional platform complexity.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Some hosts measure data transfer, while others use visitor counts or a credit system. Check how each provider calculates usage rather than comparing headline numbers alone.

If your website rebuilds whenever you publish content, deployment limits matter. A blog updated a few times a month has different requirements from an application receiving dozens of deployments every day.

Free hosting doesn't always mean you can run a business website. Vercel's Hobby plan and GitHub Pages have restrictions that may rule out certain commercial projects.

Some services include custom domains on free plans. Others require an upgrade before you can connect one.

A free plan might stop serving additional usage, while another provider may bill for overages.

Before publishing a production website, check the provider's billing behavior and configure spending controls where available.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every important page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Open Graph tags help control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support them.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Include a sitemap with the canonical URLs you want search engines to discover.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

Depending on the website, you may want Organization, Article, BreadcrumbList, or other relevant schema types.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure important pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

Cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

Yes. TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, Render, and several other services offer free hosting options. Most free plans have restrictions involving bandwidth, deployments, storage, or usage. Check the terms before using a free plan for a business website.

A small static website can cost nothing to host if it stays within a provider's free allowances. Paid plans vary from fixed monthly subscriptions to usage-based pricing. Domain registration, paid back-end services, and additional storage or bandwidth may increase the total cost.

For a standalone HTML file, upload-based hosting is generally the simplest approach. Services such as TiinyHost let you publish a file without configuring Git or a build process. If the project already lives in a GitHub repository, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages may be more convenient.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. It also supports commercial projects, making it more appropriate for some business websites that would fall outside GitHub Pages' permitted uses.

Static website hosting doesn't need to be expensive or complicated. The important part is choosing a service that matches your website and deployment process.

Cloudflare Pages is a good starting point for static websites that need generous free bandwidth. Netlify is useful for Git-based development, while GitHub Pages suits personal projects and documentation.

If you're publishing a small HTML file or sharing a prototype, upload-based hosting may be all you need.

#10373. Google Pixel Tag Initial Review: The gold standard for Find Hub trackers, whatever that’s worth

Google’s Find Hub had a tumultuous launch for its performance, but also for a lack of clear direction in hardware. Over two years later, that’s finally arriving in the Google Pixel Tag which, even just a few days in, is the obvious gold standard in the race to build an AirTag for Android devices.

Google Pixel Tag is now available for purchase at the Google Store and Amazon.

There are plenty of really good Android Find Hub trackers on the market. Pebblebee and Chipolo have been long-standing examples of how to build good dual-network trackers that work on both Android and iOS, while Motorola’s Moto Tag series has delivered two Android-only trackers that deliver better performance and more focused features. But even with the Moto Tag, there’s a clear compromise. Features like the ability to ring your phone are tied to a separate app and, in turn, have some inherent clunkiness.

Pixel Tag is the device that finally brings it all together, and it’s brilliant so far.

I’ve only had the Pixel Tag for a week and, frankly, it’s impossible to properly review a tracker in that time. There are only so many ways to artificially test out how a tracker works, as most cases where you’ll find value in this sort of product can only occur in real life.

So, with that said, let’s focus on the fundamentals.

Google Pixel Tag pairs to your Android phone just like any other Find Hub tracker – though much faster compared to some others I’ve tested – but the differences are obvious towards the end of that process. The final screen shows options for setting ringer volume and an option to set up “Ring this phone.”

Those new features are what make the Pixel Tag so good, and so appealing compared to all of the competition. A quick double-tap on the Tag’s button rings whichever phone you connected it to, assuming it’s in range, and it works pretty reliably. You can also set up “left behind” alerts (now available on other Find Hub trackers too) for when the phone leaves the tracker behind – you can set up exclusion zones such as your home or work address.

One of my favorite examples of the added polish from Google is the ability to adjust the ringer volume on the page where you actually want to ring the tracker. In a crowded but quiet space where you know the tracker is close by, being able to quickly set the volume to low is a great addition. In my book, it’s the reason to buy Pixel Tag over any other Android tracker.

UWB, of course, only makes up-close finding all the better. I found this decently reliable on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, but it is a little bit frustrating that the directional cues vanish within about 10-12 feet. Fine for a backpack or something like that, potentially a problem if your Tag is attached to a set of keys.

On that note, my biggest hardware complaint is that Google took the Apple route of having no built-in mounting mechanism. The super thin and light hardware of Pixel Tag is wonderful, don’t get me wrong, but being forced to buy a separate accessory just to attach it to my bag is frustrating! One of Google’s partners, Bellroy, built one of these accessories and it’s simple enough – a silicone case with a rope. I wish I didn’t need it, but it works, and at least you get two of them in a pack for $25.

The hardware itself is pretty good across the board, really, with the battery door also being slightly easier to open compared to the Moto Tag. Inside is a standard CR2032 battery that Google says will last “over one year.” I’d personally still prefer a rechargeable battery with USB-C or wireless charging, but this is a good enough solution given the amount of time the battery lasts – hopefully Google’s claim lives up.

Rounding out some of the key aspects here, it’s worth saying that the built-in speaker is more than loud enough at its highest setting, but the value for me so far has really come in that the low setting is actually low enough to not be a nuisance. I do find it a little strange that there’s no visual indication of where the Tag’s button is, but the packaging and app both do a good enough job of letting you know.

I really just wish it would have a rechargeable battery, preferably via USB-C. It would have been the only tracker on the market to support UWB and be rechargeable.

I’m looking forward to seeing how Pixel Tag performs as the travel season spins back up, so stay tuned for a later long-term review of Google’s tracker in the coming months. Initial impressions, though, are solid. Sound off in the comments below if you have any questions around Pixel Tag, I’ll answer everything I can!

Google Pixel Tag is now available at the Google Store and Amazon.

Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, just filed a RICO lawsuit against their county commissioners, county leaders, and OpenAI and its affiliates, alleging that they committed various offenses in a conspiracy to get OpenAI’s “Project Camellia” approved. According to the Effingham Herald, the plaintiffs — Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr., and Raymond Carver — are seeking civil damages, saying that the project has harmed their property values and even pointing out that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced.

The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners — Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly, and Phil Kieffer — as defendants, alongside County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority (IDA) CEO Brandt Herndon, the IDA itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, the entity operating the data center on behalf of OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the agency involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI.

It’s alleged that the defendants committed fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements so that residents remain unaware of the nature of the projects for as long as possible, and that there was a civil conspiracy “to advance Project Camellia through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.” They also claimed that the parties engaged in improper land transactions, zoning violations, and civil racketeering.w

Project Camellia is one of OpenAI’s biggest data center projects planned for construction in Effingham County. The site is expected to cost somewhere between $20 billion and $30 billion, to be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. The company also promised that it will not affect the community’s utility costs, as it will pay for the full cost of all its required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will have minimal water use due to its closed-loop water system. Despite those promises, it seems that some people are opposing the project because of how the county had allegedly tried to secure the land, tax incentives, and zoning approvals without informing the residents until key decisions were finalized and contracts had been signed.

The RICO Act — or Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act — was originally conceived as a way to counter organized crime, particularly Mafia leadership, who often used low-level members to commit individual crimes and do the dirty work for them. However, Georgia’s RICO Act is less stringent than the federal version, which is why it’s been used multiple times for cases that seemingly had nothing to do with the Mafia. For example, it was in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others in the attempt to overturn the 2020 U.S. presidential election results in the state, and it was also used in Young Thug’s trial after the rapper was accused of running YSL Records as a criminal street gang.

Critics say that Georgia’s version is way too encompassing, though, and that it was being used to squeeze defendants involved in more mundane or common felonies. “When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” Georgia State University professor of criminal justice and criminology Volkan Topalli said in Atlanta Magazine.

The actions of both state officials, OpenAI, and its affiliates are not new, though. There have already been multiple complaints of data center developers and local governments using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) while they negotiate terms for possible data center projects. Developers say they use this tool to avoid “running afoul of insider trading rules,” but people have pointed out that West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana was able to close a data center deal without resorting to one. An AWS data center in Gilroy, California, is also facing scrutiny after residents only discovered the nature of the project when construction began after a five-year permitting saga that relied on zoning rules that were set 45 years ago.

#10371. A remote employee refused 160 webcam photos a day. Her employer fired her

Across the workforce, employer surveillance is growing increasingly common, even though it is widely disliked by employees. According to the American Psychological Association, employee monitoring increases workers’ stress and decreases their reported mental health. A Canadian study found that surveillance in the workplace makes employees feel more pressured, less satisfied with their job, and like their privacy is being violated.

AI may now make this problem worse. These negative outcomes are the consequences of more traditional surveillance methods like keyboard tracking and email monitoring. Considering that, what would the psychological impact be of learning that an employer will now use AI to take 160 photos of an employee’s face every day?

A recent New Jersey lawsuit alleges that an employer was trying to do just that, and fired its employee when she refused to agree to this monitoring. The plaintiff in this case, Glennis Von Sander-Timinski, worked for Sutherland Healthcare Solutions, which provides healthcare services outsourcing. The suit states that she had been working at home with no issues since 2018, and had achieved positive performance reviews during that time. 

However, everything changed in August when her company told her that they would be using a new tool: Sentinel AI. This software would take a photo of her through her webcam about every three minutes over the course of the day, for a total of about 160 photos per day.

Von Sander-Timinski objected to this with the worry that it would increase her stress level, and therefore trigger her underlying lupus. According to the Lupus Foundation of America, stress can be a significant trigger of lupus flares, which can result in fevers, rashes, and sores. Her doctor wrote a note to her employer arguing that the facial AI monitoring should be changed to be “intermittent or less frequently, as it is causing worsening of anxiety and flaring her systemic lupus erythematosus.”

However, Sutherland Healthcare was not willing to compromise and gave her an ultimatum. She could agree to the AI monitoring, come into the office every day, or be fired. Returning to the office was not feasible as she lives in Atlantic County, on the opposite side of New Jersey from her employer’s office in Clinton. The lawsuit estimated that her daily commute would have been a total of six hours long.

Therefore, on September 8, Von Sander-Timinski was fired. She had worked at Sutherland for over a decade, since it acquired the company she previously worked for in 2013. 

“Our client’s employer failed to engage in the interactive process required under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and denied a reasonable accommodation that would have allowed Ms. Von Sander-Timinski to continue performing her job duties successfully, as she had done for years prior to the implementation of this monitoring system,” said Von Sander-Timinski’s lawyers in a statement to The Bergen Record.

While many states currently do not have any laws against employer surveillance, some states, such as New York, Connecticut, Delaware, and California, are beginning to set boundaries for companies. Earlier this year, Maine also passed a law that bans surveillance within an employee’s home unless it is deemed necessary.

New Jersey is similarly looking to pass a law that would regulate AI electronic monitoring tools in the workplace. It would mandate that AI-powered surveillance would need to be approved by an independent auditor and would limit where and when monitoring can be active. 

While this bill is still under discussion, it could potentially help employees like Von Sander-Timinski avoid similar situations in the future. For now, in the vast majority of states, if an employer decides to implement facial monitoring, employees will have little option but to smile for the camera.

#10369. Pixel Tag tidbits: Surprise NFC, Find Hub setup, & Bellroy keychain cases

The Made by Google 2026 lineup is finally complete with tomorrow’s retail launch of the Pixel Tag. You can find our review here, while there are some additional details about the device since the August announcement.

The Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker with NFC. Google did not mention this connectivity specification in August, with Near Field Communication letting you tap the tracker to the back of your phone to immediately open device settings. The NFC area on the Pixel Tag is below the circular battery door, which you hold down and twist counterclockwise to open.

On Android 17 QPR2, tapping immediately opens the details page. On QPR1, you first get a system notification that you need to click. NFC joins Bluetooth 6.0 with Channel Sounding and Ultra Wideband (UWB).

The setup process adds a new screen after the initial pairing and terms of use. It lets you configure: Notify when left behind, Ring this phone, Edit name, Edit category, and Adjust volume for this tag.

The Pixel Tag has a physical button on the rear side below the battery cover. Clicking twice plays a loud sound on your phone if both devices are nearby. Once found, you can tap the button once to silence, or turn it off from your phone. This feature can be disabled from the Pixel Tag’s device details page on a tracker-by-tracker basis.

Google does not have a first-party case for the Pixel Tag. Instead, it’s working with Made for Google partner Bellroy.

There are two models available from the Google Store, with the first made of silicone. The Bellroy Lite Case Duo costs $24.99 and comes in a pack of two: Mist and Shadow colorways. It wraps everything but the face of the Pixel Tag (and its speaker cutout), while giving you a hole in the corner and color-matching cord.

There’s also the Bellroy Leather Tag Case in Artichoke, Azalea, Black, Pewter, and Red Ochre for $29.99.

#10367. FAA grounds all flights in the U.S. until further notice: Reports cite air traffic control outage

In a rare move, the Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it was grounding all flights in the United States from departing “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety . . . until further notice,” according to NBC News.

The FAA reportedly issued the ground stop “due to several impacts to ATC [air traffic control] Frequencies and/or Radar capabilities,” with the FAA command center telling airlines it does not have further information on the “timing or cause of this outage,” aviation industry news service The Air Current reported.

Reached by Fast Company, the FAA pointed to a post on X from Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, saying the ground stop “follows a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

Duffy added: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, “there is no indication that we’ve had, no reason to believe, that as of right now this was a threat to the United States,” later adding, “this was a telecommunication outage,” per CNN.

According to FlightAware.com, a live flight tracker website, there are more than 9,000 flights delayed within, into, or out of the U.S. today, with 440 flights canceled (as of 5:20 p.m. ET).

“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the FAA posted on X.

The last nationwide ground stop was on January 11, 2023, when a contractor for the FAA “unintentionally deleted files related to a key pilot safety system,” according to CNN reporting at that time. The only other time such an order was issued was following the attacks on September 11, 2001.

#10364. Apple TV has a new ASL feature, offering a richer language experience beyond captions

Apple introduced a new sign language interpretation feature on Friday, alongside the premiere of the Apple TV movie Being Heumann.

The feature, designed with native signers, offers a visual of a person on the screen. Rather than replacing captions as an accessibility option, Apple is offering another function to improve users’ viewing experience through American Sign Language and British Sign Language.

People in the Deaf community have cited inability to get the full experience of watching shows and movies due to captions that lack descriptions of tone and mood. Poorly timed captions can throw off an entire episode or movie, and incorrect language can alter the understanding of a conversation.

The new feature goes hand in hand with the 2026 biographical drama directed by Sian Heder based on the memoir Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist by its namesake Judith Heumann with writer Kristen Joiner.

Starring Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien, and Ruth Madeley as Heumann, the film debuted in select theaters on November 6 and was released for streaming on Apple TV today. 

A 2021 Census Bureau presentation discussed the difficulty of collecting accurate ASL-user statistics through traditional household language surveys. The Deaf community is often undercounted in national data, making it harder to measure accessibility needs. 

Apple Originals have led the industry in providing accessibility features, such as Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing and Audio Description for blind and low-vision audiences, in multiple languages, worldwide. 

For its new feature, Apple created each interpretation with a DASL (director of artistic sign language) and an interpreter. They worked together in a studio to create high-quality sign language, capturing the tone and emotional intensity of each film being interpreted.

“I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in the movie and also directed the film’s sign language interpretation.

A new PETG ESD filament just entered the market, and it's a better value than the competition.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prusa released its new Prusament PETG ESD on Tuesday: a carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube (CNT)- filled, electrostatic-dissipative (ESD) PETG filament meant to protect static-sensitive electronics. While it’s great for enclosures for a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, and the like, Prusa is targeting the filament more toward electronics production than hobbyist use; however, it’s cheaper than the non-ESD Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber at only $56.99.

Prusa isn’t the only one selling ESD filament; 3DXTech and Polymaker were first to the scene, but Prusa is the first to include carbon fiber alongside carbon nanotubes to provide the ESD properties, improving dimensional accuracy and minimizing warping. 3DXTech sells its ESD-PETG at $105; Polymaker’s Fiberon PETG-ESD is $65.98, but the Prusament PETG ESD is only $56.99 and is the only one with carbon fiber reinforcement.

Non-ESD filaments are generally safe for electronics enclosures; many hobbyists use regular PLA, PETG, and ABS without any problems. And while the extra protection can be appreciated, Prusa positions this not for hobbyists, but for electronics production — PCB fixtures and holders for soldering, IC trays for handling and transport, holders for testing multiple boards at once, etc., as Prusa shows on the PETG ESD product page. It saves on manufacturing costs, reducing the need for CNC-machined ESD trays and fixtures, and can be quickly printed on-site with very little lead time. It’s not necessarily for big businesses only either, as indie hardware developers and smaller-scale manufacturers could use this filament to improve their production line without buying expensive ESD filament.

Prusa has not yet published the datasheet containing details about the strength of the filament, but Prusa claims that the filament has increased stiffness and reduced toughness, similar to Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber’s properties. However, the amount of carbon fiber in PETG ESD may be different from PETG Carbon Fiber, as the latter’s purpose is more for strength than for electronics manufacturing.

Prusa is known to use its own 3D printers to print its own components and use its own products for the 3D printers it sells, and on the product page, Prusa says it uses PETG ESD in its own production line to prevent overcoating the edges when powder coating its print sheets. While it isn’t the first or only ESD filament on the market, it’s certainly the cheapest, and when its strength profile is released or tested independently, it may potentially be more worth it than Prusa’s own PETG Carbon Fiber in certain cases.
